Learning Objectives
Review the basic concepts of informed consent.
Summarize the informed consent process.
Assess the legal implications of informed consent.
Discuss common pitfalls in acquiring informed consent.
Evaluate special considerations in acquiring informed consent.
Overview
Healthcare providers are ethically and legally obligated to acquire informed consent from a
patient before treatment.

Informed consent is based on the central tenet of patient autonomy. A patient’s decision
making cannot be obstructed by outside influences or lack of understanding regarding the
procedure/treatment.
Healthcare providers must be aware of a patient’s level of education and have an in-depth
knowledge of the procedure/treatment to ensure risks and advantages are adequately
discussed.

Overview
Informed consent is the process in which a healthcare provider teaches a patient about
the indications, risks, advantages, and alternative treatment options for a particular
treatment or procedure.1 The informed consent process is based on the tenet of patient
autonomy, which states that a patient’s decision making should be free from the
influence of others and from barriers, such as incomplete understanding, that hinder
free choice.2 The informed consent process is not only an ethical obligation but also a
legal requirement and is important in the patient-doctor relationship.3 Legal precedent
over the past century has moved away from the physician-led beneficence model of
clinical judgment and has heavily favored patient autonomy and decision making.4 In
clinical practice, several factors may add ambiguity to the process. Healthcare providers
must be aware of a patient’s level of education and language abilities and have an in-
depth knowledge of the procedure to ensure the risks and advantages are adequately
discussed.5 Patients must demonstrate competence and a clear understanding of the
procedure or treatment.
The Process
Consent is required before treatment, a procedure, surgery, blood transfusion, anesthesia, or
sharing patient information.
An informed consent must review the procedure or treatment, evaluate alternative treatment
options, and stress potential risks and advantages.
Teach-back methods should be used to help determine patient comprehension and aid in
information retention by the patient.


The Process
Medical professionals must obtain informed consent before initiating treatment,
procedures, surgery, and blood transfusions; administering anesthesia; and sharing
patient information.1 The methodology for obtaining informed consent varies among
surgeons and among the patients of an individual surgeon.6,7 Typically, this process
involves a verbal discussion and obtaining the patient’s signature to affirm the patient’s
consent; however, more recently, videos and computer software have been used in
acquiring consent. Acquiring informed consent from a patient requires several steps,
and clear communication is necessary to minimize patient harm.8,9 These steps include
ascertaining if the patient is competent, explaining the indication for a given procedure,
reviewing the risks and advantages of the procedure, and elaborating on alternative
treatment options.
To give consent, the patient must be an adult. For children, consent must be obtained
from a parent or legal guardian. Patient competence must be assessed, and the medical
provider must ensure that medications that impair decision making have not been
administered.10,11 Classes of medication to be aware of include but are not limited to
benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and opiates. After the determination of patient
competence, the surgeon must begin by describing the treatment or procedure to the
patient in an easy-to-comprehend manner. The patient must be made aware of his or
her participation and that an equitable joint decision-making model is followed. The
surgeon must highlight all feasible alternative treatment options before discussing
potential risks for the proposed treatment option. The patient’s final decision is indicated
by a signature on the consent forms. Consent is not valid if the patient does not have a
clear understanding of the procedure, alternative treatment options, and risk after the
treatment. Using teach-back methods substantially improves patient understanding of
the procedure. In a randomized control trial, Wadey and Frank12 evaluated 20 patients
who underwent elective anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. Patients were
separated into two cohorts: one that participated in the standard informed consent
process and another that was required to verbalize the risks and advantages of the
procedure during the consent process. At a follow-up of 1 month, the authors found that
patients in the experimental group were able to recall all risks and advantages compared

with only four patients in the standard group (P = 0.03). In 2010, the National Quality
Forum published updated Safe Practices for Better Health Care, which highlighted 30 key
practices that improve patient safety.13,14 Safe Practice No. 10 stresses the importance
of the teach-back method during the informed consent process, allowing the surgeon to
gauge a patient’s understanding and enabling increased information retention in
patients, even if literacy is limited.
Legal Implications
Several legal standards are used for adequate informed consent. These include but are not
limited to the reasonable physician standard and the reasonable person standard.
The legal standard for informed consent continues to evolve and change based on jurisdiction.
Informed consent serves to protect patients from assault and battery by preventing unwanted
medical treatment and also aids in protecting surgeons from future litigation.
The most common allegation pertaining to informed consent involves a failure to adequately
explain alternative treatment options and a failure to explain risks associated with a given
treatment option.
Factors shown to substantially reduce indemnity risk include informed consent obtained by
the primary surgeon and obtained in an ambulatory care setting.

Legal Implications
Before the 20th century, patient consent was legally bound by informal patient
agreement; however, this changed during the landmark case of Schloendorff versus The
Society of New York Hospital in 1914.4 In this case, the patient had consented to undergo
examination under anesthesia but clearly expressed that no surgical treatment was to
be performed. During the procedure, a mass was found. To minimize risk to the patient
of undergoing anesthesia a second time, the surgeon opted to excise the mass.
Complications related to the excision occurred in the patient, who subsequently filed a
lawsuit against the surgeon. Although the surgeon opted to act in what he believed to
the best interest of the patient, the courts ruled that “every human being of adult years
and sound mind has a right to determine what shall be done with his body.” In the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Informed Consent
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002008
4/13

1950s, the courts ruled in favor of the reasonable physician standard, which predicates
that a physician must disclose information about the procedure that any reasonable
physician would disclose.15 In the 1970s, the case of Canterbury versus Spence introduced
the reasonable person standard, which required that clinicians disclose information
regarding a procedure that any reasonable person undergoing the procedure would
want to know.16
Currently, in an increasingly litigious environment, the informed consent process serves
as a legal safeguard to document the interaction between a clinician and his or her
patient.17 This documentation legally protects patients from an assault and battery
experience by unwanted medical treatment and also aids in protecting surgeons from
future litigation. In a claims analysis of 243 orthopaedics cases, 5.3% of the cases
involved inadequate informed consent.18 To evaluate the informed consent process
from a legal preceptive, Bhattacharyya et al19 performed a closed claims analysis of 28
lawsuits with claims of inadequate informed consent. All the cases involved elective
orthopaedic surgical procedures; none were emergent cases. The authors reported that
obtaining informed consent in the ambulatory care setting and documenting it in office
notes resulted in a significant reduction in indemnity risk (P < 0.01). The authors also
revealed that informed consent obtained in an ambulatory care setting by the primary
surgeon resulted in a significant decrease in indemnity risk compared with if it was
obtained by other members of the healthcare team (P < 0.01). In addition, the study
highlighted that informed consent obtained on the wards or in the preoperative area
was associated with increased indemnity risk (P < 0.01). Grauberger et al20 performed a
retrospective cohort study of 233 patients who underwent spinal surgery and filed
malpractice claims because of inadequate informed consent. The authors found that the
mean interval between the date of surgery and the date of the verdict was 5.7 years
(interquartile range, 4 to 7 years). The most common allegation was failure to explain
alternative treatment options (9.9% of cases) and risks associated with the given
procedure (30.4% of cases). To avoid litigation, surgeons must provide concise informed
consent and ensure adequate patient understanding.
The legal standard for informed consent continues to evolve, and standards change
based on jurisdiction.21 Physicians should be aware of the standards in their area of
practice and tailor the process to meet the requirements.

Common Pitfalls
Although supplemental material aids in the informed consent process, such material typically
is beyond the recommended sixth-grade reading level.
Bilingual surgeons at many institutions underestimate the language barrier between
themselves and their patients.
Surgeons must realize that culture influences a patient’s understanding and that patients of
similar nationalities or who speak similar languages may not share the same cultural values.
A patient’s health literacy may hinder his or her ability to make informed medical discussions.

Common Pitfalls
Because of the complexity of contemporary medical treatment and procedures, the
informed consent process has become increasingly important to ensure patient safety
and satisfaction. Evaluation of common issues that physicians encounter in obtaining
informed consent is essential. During the informed consent process, patients often are
given pamphlets or documents to explain key aspects of a given procedure.
Seewoonarain et al22 examined the readability of 58 pamphlets provided by seven
orthopaedic associations. The authors found that, based on the Flesch-Kincaid Grade
Level Readability test, the mean reading level of the pamphlets was that of an individual
aged 15 years. Based on the Simple Measure of Gobbledygook test, the mean reading
level of the pamphlets was that of an individual aged 17 years. The authors indicated
that the mean reading level of their patient population was age 12 years and that the
pamphlets contained increasingly complex language that patients may have difficulty
understanding. Roberts et al23 assessed the readability of patient education material
developed by the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons and reported that only
3.9% of the provided material was at or below the recommended sixth-grade reading
level. This illustrates that, although supplemental material is useful in aiding the
informed consent process, it cannot function as a replacement for a careful explanation
from the primary surgeon. In an increasingly multicultural and multilingual society, a
surgeon must be sensitive to patient factors, such as native language, cultural beliefs,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Informed Consent
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002008
6/13

and level of health literacy, because they play a vital role in patient understanding during
the informed consent process.9 In a sample of 50 hospitals, Wilson-Stronks et al24
reported that only 37% of hospitals required bilingual staff to display competency before
serving as an interpreter during a patient interaction. The authors reported that this has
led to the underestimation of language barriers by clinicians at many institutions. To
overcome this problem, the authors recommended the use of healthcare interpretive
services during all informed consent processes for patients with limited English
proficiency. Providers must realize that culture influences a patient’s understanding of
the world and that patients of similar nationalities or who speak similar languages may
not share the same cultural values. To assess the effect of cultural diversity on informed
consent, Lakes et al25 set up focus groups with representatives from six cultures in
Orange County, California. The authors found that cultural belief played a considerable
role in patient medical decision making and was routinely discussed as a factor
influencing consent. To overcome the cultural barriers during the informed consent
process, the authors recommended community contribution in developing consent
forms and educational materials. The Joint Commission26 highlighted that a patient’s
health literacy can hinder her or her ability to make informed medical discussions. To
remedy this issue, the Joint Commission strongly encourages the use of plain language,
teach-back methods, drawings, and models, as well as limiting details to one or two
critical items at a time during the informed consent process.
Special Considerations
Patients younger than 17 years cannot provide informed consent. With the exception of
emancipated minors, an in-depth conversation must be held with the parents of the minor
who will be providing informed consent.
Informed consent can be foregone in the case of voluntarily waived consent; incapacitated
patients; or life-threatening, time-sensitive conditions.
To obtain consent from patients with a mental disability who have no family or guardian, a
court order must be requested before performing any procedure.

Special Considerations

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002008
7/13

Patients younger than 17 years are considered children and legally cannot provide
informed consent. In dealing with minors, the provider must have an in-depth
conversation with the minor’s parents, who will ultimately be providing informed
consent.27 If a minor is under the care of a legal guardian, proof of guardianship must be
demonstrated. These rules do not apply to legally emancipated minors. Examples of
criteria that meet the requirement for legal emancipation include individuals who are
married and younger18 years, individuals serving in the military, individuals mothering
children, and individuals demonstrating financial independence.28 Legislation regarding
the consent process for minors varies on a state-by-state basis, and surgeons should be
aware of the laws in their state.
Although informed consent is a central tenet of patient-centered care, situations arise in
which informed consent can be waived. Obtaining informed consent is not required
from patients who have voluntarily waived consent or who are incapacitated or if
emergent, time-sensitive conditions threatening life or limb arise. In requiring informed
consent from an incapacitated patient, the operating surgeon and a colleague of similar
knowledge and experience can document the appropriate treatment and forgo the
consent process.29 In evaluating patient comprehension after informed consent during a
myocardial infarction, Yuval et al30 reported that only 31% of patients demonstrated full
comprehension, 50% of patients had partial comprehension, and 19% of patients had no
comprehension. The authors also learned that the duration of the consent process
correlated with patient comprehension (P <0.01), suggesting that brevity of the consent
process in an urgent/emergent setting hinders patient understanding. Although this
study demonstrated that the brevity of the informed consent process in emergent
situations may hinder patients from providing proper informed consent, many patients
still had decision-making capacity. Therefore, the physician and the patient must have an
appropriate dialogue.
To obtain informed consent from a mentally disabled patient who has no family or
guardian, a court must review the case and provide a court order to proceed with any
treatment. Some institutions have review committees that evaluate these cases to
circumvent a time-consuming court process. The use of committee discussions protects
the treating physician from liability.31

In addition, special consideration must be made for patients consenting to participate in
clinical research. Before obtaining consent for research purposes, institutional review
board approval must be obtained.32 In obtaining informed consent from potential
research participants, patients must be provided with adequate information about the
study involvement to allow for informed decision making. Patients should understand
that study protocols may differ from the standard of care, they may not benefit from the
proposed therapies, and they may be exposed to unknown adverse events. Code of
Federal Regulations Title 21 provided by the FDA mandates that patients be given
adequate time to consider their participation, ample time be provided to answer any
questions patients may have, and efforts be made to minimize patient coercion.
Obtaining informed consent for research purposes can be waived if the study does not
transgress on the patient’s right to self-determination, the study is of high clinical
importance, and obtaining an informed consent has been demonstrated to be
unfeasible.33 For example, informed consent can be waived without impeding a patient’s
right to self-determination in the single-consent model.34 The single-consent model
applies to randomized controlled trials with control groups receiving the standard of
care. Participants can be randomized before the consent process, and the control group
may be exempt from obtaining consent because their autonomy regarding treatment
options has not been affected. Examples of situations in which obtaining informed
consent is considered unfeasible include if the process requires a large expenditure of
time and economic resources, if obtaining consent influences the validity of the study,
and during emergent situations investigating lifesaving treatment options.35,36
